title: 2026-11-25 Harbor Health Analytics — LLM port & orchestration roadmap to Redwood
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Harbor Health through a migration roadmap from current OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API. Focus areas: parity mapping of model outputs, console rollout (canary/A-B), VPC/private options, KMS/entropy for PHI, performance tuning (batching, quantization, KV prefix caching), and cost tradeoffs. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot benchmark with a 10K request/day profile; Redwood to share pricing and SOC2 docs plus a preliminary runbook.
action_items: Jordan: Send tailored pricing + SOC2 & ISO docs by 2026-11-27
Maya: Share initial pilot runbook and benchmark template by 2026-11-30
Ravi: Provide sample payloads and 24-hour traffic trace (anonymized) by 2026-11-29
Samira: Confirm networking constraints (eg. egress, allowed IP ranges) by 2026-12-02
next_steps: Redwood to provision trial API key and starter config for parity tests
Customer to sign non-prod pilot NDA and upload sample logs
Schedule 1-hour benchmark kickoff with SREs on 2026-12-01
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-25 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Soto (CTO), Ravi Patel (ML Eng), Samira Ghosh (SRE), Tomas Reed (Product)

[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood Inference, with Maya and Liam on the SE side. how's Harbor doing today?
[00:12] Dr. Elena: good thanks, lots going on, we've been evaluating vendor consolidation, so this is timed well.
[00:20] Ravi: hi, we'll jump into the technical bits — we currently run a mix of OpenAI for chat and Anthropic for higher-safety scoring, also a few Together models for long context. main ask: parity and predictable cost.
[00:33] Maya (SE): great, that matches what we prepared. quick agenda: parity mapping, console + rollout, private/VPC options, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quant. we'll run through a live parity example too.
[00:45] Tomas: curious about any gotchas in function calling and streaming — our product uses both.
[00:52] Maya: yep we'll demo function calling shim and streaming behavior, there are some small differences but we have patterns to keep behavior identical.
[01:10] Liam: also pointing out that sometimes model outputs tokenization can shift scoring — we'll show a deterministic temperature/echo mapping.
[01:25] Dr. Elena: ok let's jump in.
[01:35] [02:00] (screen share begins — console)
[02:05] Maya: this is the Redwood Console — per-route dashboards, token breakdowns, and a parity mapping panel we use during onramp. here we have an OpenAI->Redwood mapping for gpt-4-ish class to "rwd-gptx-1" and Anthropic-claiborne mapping to our safety-tuned family.
[02:30] Ravi: how are you handling prompt-engineering differences? sometimes completions truncate, or stop tokens differ.
[02:42] Maya: good Q — we do a 3-step parity tactic: 1) tokenizer normalization (we run a pre-token normalize step), 2) response shaping rules (trailing whitespace/stop handling), 3) small post-processing rules in the SDK. many teams embed that in a microservice, some use our SDK hooks.
[03:05] Samira: networking — we need VPC egress control, can you run in our VPC or do you require open egress?
[03:16] Jordan: we offer Private (customer VPC) and on-prem packages. for Private we deploy a control plane with customer-managed network and KMS integrations. egress can be locked to your IP ranges.
[03:30] Tomas: does that support HSM / vault?
[03:35] Maya: yes KMS/HSM via our integrations — you manage the keys. there is an audit log stream available for all token-level events.
[03:48] [04:00] (parity demo — sample chat prompt)
[04:05] Maya: here's a real prompt from Harbor's product: "Summarize patient's notes and flag follow-up items" — we ran it against your Anthropic endpoint and mapped to rwd-safety-x. result characters are nearly identical; slight punctuation differences.
[04:30] Ravi: I see differences in list formatting — would that break our extractor?
[04:35] Maya: we include a structured-output option and function-calling semantics that mimic the provider's JSON outputs; if you rely on exact punctuation we can add a rule to preserve list markers.
[04:50] Dr. Elena: what about streaming token latency? we need sub-200ms first-byte for short replies.
[05:02] Liam: for hosted low-latency workloads we hit ~80-150ms first byte on regional clusters for short prompts; for heavy context or KV cache misses it's higher. we can configure dedicated capacity to tighten SLOs.
[05:20] Ravi: you mentioned KV cache — our application uses long context and we rely heavily on KV cache across requests. how does Redwood's cache compare?
[05:32] Maya: our KV cache is continuous and prefix-aware; we store token KV and have both per-request and global prefix caching. we've seen 30-60% token cost reduction for convo-heavy apps. sometimes transcripts show K-V cash in notes — sorry transcription is rough — but it's a proper KV cache.
[05:55] Samira: for compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001, data residency?
[06:03] Jordan: we are SOC 2 Type II and have ISO artifacts; we can provide evidence and map controls. for residency we can pin regions or run Private in your VPC.
[06:18] Tomas: what's the pilot profile you suggest?
[06:22] Maya: we recommend a 2-week pilot: mirror ~10k req/day production mix, run parity tests and plus latency/cost baselines. Redwood provides instrumentation and a benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:38] Dr. Elena: sounds good. what about quantization — we've seen accuracy regressions in some quantized variants.
[06:48] Liam: Optimize gives per-model quant recommendations by workload; we surface reg rates on evals and can recommend mixed-precision or 4-bit with LUTs. we can also run an eval harness with your prompts to measure regression.
[07:05] Ravi: can we keep Anthropic for safety-critical flows and switch everything else? partial migration is our likely approach.
[07:14] Jordan: absolutely — routing policies let you route by policy: safety tier, latency, cost. you can run split traffic, canaries, and automatic fallback to a safety model.
[07:28] [08:00] (deep-technical Q&A)
[08:10] Samira: our SREs want to run a preflight: synthetic traffic, token distribution, and a cold-start test. do you have tooling?
[08:22] Maya: yes we have a synthetic runner and a cold-start trace tool; also console traces let you see KV cache hits and batching histograms.
[08:35] Ravi: SDK changes — do we have to rewrite all client code?
[08:40] Liam: no, we provide adapter shims for OpenAI/Anthropic/Together APIs, plus native SDKs. many customers get away with a 2-file shim and some small post-processing.
[08:55] Dr. Elena: function calling differences again — Together's approach is different shape-wise.
[09:03] Maya: we have a compatibility layer for function calling; caveat: if you rely on implicit tool selection heuristics, we'll need a small mapping table.
[09:20] [10:00] (pricing and cost model)
[10:05] Jordan: quick on cost — the console shows per-token cost breakdown and cost for embeddings/recall. Dedicated gives unit economics predictability; hosted is lower friction. Optimize suggests batching and prefix caching to reduce cost.
[10:25] Tomas: is there an expected drop in p95 latency when batching?
[10:30] Liam: batching helps throughput more than single-request p95; with continuous batching we can keep latency SLOs while improving cost. for sub-200ms p95 you may need smaller batch windows on dedicated nodes.
[10:50] Ravi: any vendor lock-in if we use Redwood SDK features?
[10:55] Jordan: our SDKs are optional. we provide adapter shims so you can revert back to provider's API if needed. rollouts are config-driven, not code-locked.
[11:10] [11:30] (questions from Product)
[11:35] Tomas: error handling — do you surface granular error codes for token limits vs rate limits?
[11:40] Maya: yes console groups errors: rate, quota, model-fallbacks; we also emit trace IDs you can correlate with logs.
[11:50] Samira: SSO and RBAC — we need SCIM sync and SAML 2.0.
[11:55] Jordan: supported — we integrate with SSO providers and support SCIM provisioning and role-based policies.
[12:10] Dr. Elena: one final thing — audit trail parity. regulators want per-request auditability and redactable logs.
[12:18] Maya: we have redactable audit logs and an exportable trail for compliance; you control retention and masking rules.
[12:35] [13:00] (recap & next steps)
[13:05] Jordan: recap — Redwood will: share SOC2/ISO package + pilot runbook, provision trial API key, and route a pilot. Harbor will: provide anonymized traffic traces, confirm networking constraints and sign pilot NDA.
[13:22] Dr. Elena: we'll get the artifacts to you. thanks, this was helpful.
[13:30] Jordan: great — we'll get the docs over. any other quick q?
[13:36] Ravi: one note — for long context we might ask for custom kernel tweaks, are those supported?
[13:42] Liam: yes, on Dedicated we can tune kernel/sequence optimizations; we'll add that to the runbook.
[13:55] (meeting end)

Notes on transcript: occasional mislabels and auto transcription quirks (eg "K-V cash" instead of KV cache, "claiborne" instead of Anthropic safety family), filler words kept.
